title: Milta Nahi Khuda Kabhi Insaan Ke Bagair | Ishq-e-Haqeeqi | Sufi Kalam
description:
Milta Nahi Khuda Kabhi Insaan Ke Bagair — a thought-provoking Sufi Kalam exploring Ishq, Maarefat, Irfan, and the deeper mysteries of spiritual understanding.

“Milta nahi khuda kabhi insaan ke bagair,
Haasil na hogi maarefat irfan ke bagair.”

These powerful verses invite us to look beyond the surface of religion, knowledge, and worldly appearances, and reflect on the relationship between love, humanity, and spiritual realization.

✨ THE MESSAGE OF THIS SUFI KALAM

Through mystical poetry and soulful alaap, this kalam explores the idea that the path of Ishq has its own language and that true spiritual understanding requires more than outward knowledge alone.

“Aashiq namaaz padhte hain azaan ke bagair…”

The verses use striking poetic imagery to describe the inner world of a lover whose heart is immersed in Ishq. They invite reflection on the difference between outward observance and inward devotion, and on the role of love, humility, and spiritual awareness in the seeker's journey.

The line “Ek aur bhi Quran hai Quran ke bagair” uses provocative mystical imagery to point toward inner understanding and Irfan; it should be understood in the poetic context of the kalam, not as a replacement for the Holy Quran.

“Haasil na hogi maarefat irfan ke bagair…”

A reminder to look within, deepen our understanding, and approach the mysteries of the heart with sincerity and humility.

title: Naseema Janib-e-Batha Guzar Kun ﷺ | A Soulful Farsi Naat | Maulana Jami
description:
Naseema Janib-e-Batha Guzar Kun — a timeless Persian Naat filled with love, longing, and heartfelt devotion to the Beloved Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

“نسیما جانب بطحا گذر کن
ز احوالم محمد را خبر کن”

Naseema Janib-e-Batha Guzar Kun,
Ze Ahwaalam Muhammad Ra Khabar Kun.

“O gentle breeze, pass by the land of Batha,
And convey the news of my condition to Muhammad ﷺ.”

Traditionally attributed to Maulana Abdur Rahman Jami, this beautiful Farsi Naat expresses the longing of a heart that yearns for the blessed presence of the Prophet ﷺ and seeks the mercy and grace associated with visiting his sacred resting place.

✨ THE SPIRIT OF THIS KALAM

Through its poetic Persian verses, this Naat gives voice to a soul longing to be remembered, a heart seeking relief from its pain, and a devotee hoping for the blessing of a visit to Madinah.

“Tu'i Sultan-e-Aalam Ya Muhammad,
Ze Roo-e-Lutf Soo-e-Man Nazar Kun.”

“You are the sovereign of the worlds, O Muhammad ﷺ;
Cast a gracious glance in my direction.”

The kalam also speaks of spiritual yearning and the hope for another outpouring of divine generosity:

“Musharraf Garche Shud Jami Ze Lutfash,
Khudaya Een Karam Bare Digar Kun.”

A soulful expression of devotion, this Persian Naat invites listeners to pause, reflect, and reconnect with the love of the Prophet ﷺ.

title: Saghar Mein Tere Saqi | La Khawfun Wala Yahzanoon | Sufi Kalam
description:
Sagar Mein Tere Saqi | Dil Ka Sukoon Dekha | Sufi Kalam

سَاغَر میں تِرے ساقی، دِل کا سُکُون دیکھا  
لا خَوْف آج خُود کو، لا یَحْزَنُون دیکھا

“Sagar Mein Tere Saqi, Dil Ka Sukoon Dekha” is a soulful Urdu Sufi Kalam reflecting on inner peace, spiritual love, and the experience of finding comfort in the presence of the Beloved.

Through the symbolic imagery of the Sagar (cup) and Saqi (cupbearer), this Kalam explores the journey from restlessness to peace, from longing to spiritual fulfillment, and from fear and grief toward a heart strengthened by faith.

The recurring words “La Khawfun Wala Yahzanoon” express a profound theme of freedom from fear and sorrow. Combined with expressive vocals, a benjo introduction, and an extended “Allah Hu” vocal outro, this rendition creates an atmosphere for reflection and remembrance.

Featured verses:

سَاغَر میں تِرے ساقی، دِل کا سُکُون دیکھا

تُو نے پِلایا جِن کو، دَستِ حِنا سے ہَنس کر  
اَوروں سے اَور اُن کا، دَشتِ جُنوں دیکھا

ہُنَرِ مَسِیح میں تھا، مُردوں کو جاں دینا  
پَر جاں کو جان دینا، تِرا فُنُون دیکھا

مَن عَرَفَ کا اِشارہ، بَر حَق ہے ساقی، تِیرا  
رَبِّ جَلِیل کا گھر، دِل کے دُرُون دیکھا

What does “Sagar Mein Tere Saqi” mean?

As a poetic expression, it can be rendered as: “O Saqi, in your cup I witnessed the peace of the heart.” The verse uses the imagery of the cupbearer and cup to express an experience of deep inner tranquility.

What does “La Khawfun Wala Hum Yahzanoon” mean?

It means, “There will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.” The phrase echoes Quranic wording associated with freedom from fear and sorrow.

What is the theme of this Sufi Kalam?

The Kalam reflects on spiritual peace, devotion, the heart's inner journey, and the hope of reaching a state beyond fear and grief.

title: Yaar Ko Hum Ne Ja Baja Dekha | Sufi Kalam | Wahdat-ul-Wujood | Qalb e Mast
description:
Yaar Ko Hum Ne Ja Baja Dekha | Sufi Kalam | Wahdat-ul-Wujood | Qalb e Mast

“Yaar ko hum ne ja baja dekha,"
"Kahin zahir kahin chhupa dekha,”

A profound expression of Sufi poetry about the Beloved who appears everywhere, sometimes visible, sometimes hidden. This soulful Kalam explores divine presence, the mystery of fana and baqa, the meaning of Ana-al-Haq, and the many forms through which the seeker experiences the Beloved.

Through powerful Urdu poetry, this Kalam invites us to reflect on love, devotion, selflessness, and the hidden mysteries of spiritual existence.

Featured verses:

یار کو ہم نے جا بجا دیکھا  
کہیں ظاہر کہیں چھپا دیکھا

کہیں ممکن ہوا کہیں واجب  
کہیں فانی کہیں بقا دیکھا

دید اپنی کی تھی اُسے خواہش  
آپ کو ہر طرح بنا دیکھا

شمع ہو کر کے اور پروانہ  
آپ کو آپ میں جلا دیکھا

کر کے دعویٰ کہیں انا الحق کا  
بر سر دار پر کھینچا دیکھا

کہیں عابد بنا کہیں زاہد  
کہیں رندوں کا پیشوا دیکھا

What does “Yaar Ko Hum Ne Ja Baja Dekha” mean?

It means, “I saw the Beloved everywhere, sometimes visible and sometimes hidden.” The verse reflects a Sufi search for the Beloved beyond outward appearances.

What is the meaning of “Ana-al-Haq”?

“Ana-al-Haq” means “I am the Real” or “I am the Truth.” In Sufi history, the expression is associated with Mansur al-Hallaj and is discussed in the context of mystical experience, spiritual identity, and divine reality.

What do fana and baqa mean in Sufism?

Fana commonly refers to the annihilation of the ego or self-centered identity, while baqa refers to abiding or subsisting in spiritual awareness after that transformation.
